newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Aznar defers to courts on "dirty war".
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar defers to courts on "dirty war".

text.p: Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, struggling to mend a split in his party, dodged questions on Monday on whether his Socialist predecessor Felipe Gonzalez had resorted to state terrorism to fight Basque guerrillas.
"I'm here to govern, not to try people. Justice is up to the courts," Aznar told a television interviewer when questioned on a "dirty war" that killed nearly 30 people from 1983 to 1987.
Asked whether the campaign had been run by a "Mr. X" -- possibly a pseudonym for his predecessor Felipe Gonzalez -- the prime minister replied: "Only the courts must know that."

Splits in Aznar's conservative Popular Party became evident on Sunday when its founder Manuel Fraga, a former minister under the late dictator Francisco Franco, said anti-guerrilla actions could not count as state terrorism even if they were illegal.

Fraga's statements contrasted sharply with those of Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos, who last week accused Gonzalez of having waged "bodeguilla terrorism" from a wine cellar in his official residence where he entertained friends and hatched strategies with his aides.
The Supreme Court is considering whether to summon Gonzalez, who was in power from 1982 until May this year, over the 1983-87 campaign of kidnappings, bombings, torture and murder.

The Socialist leader has denied any role in the illegal drive against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), a separatist rebel group that has killed nearly 800 people in a drive for independence launched in 1968. His first interior minister and other senior officials are on trial for the "dirty war".

Aznar narrowly beat Gonzalez in a March election after a campaign centred on this and other scandals. He has since toned down his charges and refused courts' requests to declassify military files on the anti-ETA campaign.
Pressed on whether or not the unlawful campaign had amounted to state terrorism, Aznar told his interviewer: "The former rulers face 28 court cases (for murder). Let the judges decide."
